title.en: Ares Comes to His Mother: The Battle of Staves at Papremis
title.zh: 阿瑞斯探母：帕普雷米斯的棍戰

region.en: Papremis, Nile Delta, Egypt (festival of the war-god)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲帕普雷米斯（戰神祭日）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.63 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 62-63

summary.en: At the festival of the war-god (Ares) at Papremis, the image is drawn in its shrine toward the temple while a thousand men with clubs block the gate — for the god, once grown away from his mother, had to fight his way past her temple attendants to visit her; hence, say the priests, the ritual combat in his honor, in which heads are broken and (Egyptians insist) no one dies.
summary.zh: 帕普雷米斯戰神祭日，神像乘車欲入神廟，千名持棍者封門相拒——蓋因神自幼離母，長成後欲探母而不獲准入，遂引外人破門而入。祭司稱：此棍戰之禮即由此而立，且謂傷者眾而死者無。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ethnographic myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. 'ritual-origin' is the intended topic tag; see ledger note.

passages.text: At Papremis they do sacrifice and worship as elsewhere, and besides that, when the sun begins to go down, while some few of the priests are occupied with the image of the god, the greater number of them stand in the entrance of the temple with wooden clubs, and other persons to the number of more than a thousand men with purpose to perform a vow, these also having all of them staves of wood, stand in a body opposite to those: and the image, which is in a small shrine of wood covered over with gold, they take out on the day before to another sacred building.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.63.

passages.text: The few then who have been left about the image, draw a wain with four wheels, which bears the shrine and the image that is within the shrine, and the other priests standing in the gateway try to prevent it from entering, and the men who are under a vow come to the assistance of the god and strike them, while the others defend themselves. Then there comes to be a hard fight with staves, and they break one another's heads, and I am of opinion that many even die of the wounds they receive; the Egyptians however told me that no one died.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.63.

passages.text: This solemn assembly the people of the place say that they established for the following reason: — the mother of Ares, they say, used to dwell in this temple, and Ares, having been brought up away from her, when he grew up came thither desiring to visit his mother, and the attendants of his mother's temple, not having seen him before, did not permit him to pass in, but kept him away; and he brought men to help him from another city and handled roughly the attendants of the temple, and entered to visit his mother. Hence, they say, this exchange of blows has become the custom in honour of Ares upon his festival.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.63.

title.en: The Voyage to Bubastis: Egypt's Wildest Festival
title.zh: 赴布巴斯提斯之舟：埃及最狂歡的節日

region.en: Nile from the Delta towns to Bubastis (temple of Bastet, Greek Artemis)
region.zh: 尼羅河自三角洲諸城至布巴斯提斯（貝斯特/阿爾忒彌斯神廟）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.59-60 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 59-60

summary.en: The greatest of Egypt's pilgrim feasts: men and women sail to Bubastis together in one boat, women rattling sistra, men piping; at every riverside town the women jeer at the shore-women and dance, some pulling up their garments; at Bubastis more wine is drunk in the festival than in the rest of the year, and, the natives say, seven hundred myriads of people gather yearly.
summary.zh: 埃及最盛大的朝節：男女同舟赴布巴斯提斯，婦人搖鈴，男子吹笛；沿途每城，船上的女人向岸上的女人叫喊戲謔，且舞且起衣；至布巴斯提斯，一節所耗之酒多於全年其餘時日——當地人稱歲歲聚者達七十萬眾。

sensitivity.note: Ancient festival description via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The Egyptians hold their solemn assemblies not once in the year but often, especially and with the greatest zeal and devotion at the city of Bubastis for Artemis, and next at Busiris for Isis; for in this last-named city there is a very great temple of Isis, and this city stands in the middle of the Delta of Egypt; now Isis is in the tongue of the Hellenes Demeter: thirdly, they have a solemn assembly at the city of Sais for Athene, fourthly at Heliopolis for the Sun (Helios), fifthly at the city of Buto in honour of Leto, and sixthly at the city of Papremis for Ares.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.59.

passages.text: Now, when they are coming to the city of Bubastis they do as follows: — they sail men and women together, and a great multitude of each sex in every boat; and some of the women have rattles and rattle with them, while some of the men play the flute during the whole time of the voyage, and the rest, both women and men, sing and clap their hands; and when as they sail they come opposite to any city on the way they bring the boat to land, and some of the women continue to do as I have said, others cry aloud and jeer at the women in that city, some dance, and some stand up and pull up their garments. This they do by every city along the river-bank; and when they come to Bubastis they hold festival celebrating great sacrifices, and more wine of grapes is consumed upon that festival than during the whole of the rest of the year. To this place (so say the natives) they come together year by year even to the number of seventy myriads of men and women, besides children.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.60.

title.en: The Black Doves of Thebes: The Origin of the Oracles

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of Zeus/Amon; whence the oracle-priestesses were carried)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（宙斯/阿蒙神廟；神諭女祭司自此被擄）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.54-57 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 54-57

summary.en: The priests of Theban Zeus/Amon claim two consecrated women were carried off by Phoenicians, one sold to Libya, one to Greece — founding the oracles of Ammon and of Dodona; the Dodona priestesses themselves say two black doves flew from Thebes, one to an oak at Dodona speaking with human voice, one bidding the Libyans make an oracle; Herodotus half-believes: the 'doves' were Egyptian women, whose foreign speech sounded like birds.
summary.zh: 底比斯阿蒙祭司稱：兩名侍神女子被腓尼基人擄走，一售利比亞、一售希臘——分別創立阿蒙與多多納神諭；多多納女祭司則言：兩隻黑鴿自底比斯飛出，一落橡樹作人言，一令利比亞人立神諭。希羅多德半信半疑：『鴿』實為埃及女子，其異語聽來如鳥啼。

sensitivity.note: Ancient origin myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: The priests of the Theban Zeus told me that two women in the service of the temple had been carried away from Thebes by Phenicians, and that they had heard that one of them had been sold to go into Libya and the other to the Hellenes; and these women, they said, were they who first founded the prophetic seats among the nations which have been named: and when I inquired whence they knew so perfectly of this tale which they told, they said in reply that a great search had been made by the priests after these women, and that they had not been able to find them, but they had heard afterwards this tale about them which they were telling.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.54.

passages.text: They say that two black doves flew from Thebes to Egypt, and came one of them to Libya and the other to their land. And this latter settled upon an oak-tree and spoke with human voice, saying that it was necessary that a prophetic seat of Zeus should be established in that place; and they supposed that that was of the gods which was announced to them, and made one accordingly: and the dove which went away to the Libyans, they say, bade the Libyans to make an Oracle of Ammon; and this also is of Zeus.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.55.

passages.text: Moreover, I think that the women were called doves by the people of Dodona for the reason that they were Barbarians and because it seemed to them that they uttered voice like birds; but after a time (they say) the dove spoke with human voice, that is when the woman began to speak so that they could understand; but so long as she spoke a Barbarian tongue she seemed to them to be uttering voice like a bird: for had it been really a dove, how could it speak with human voice? And in saying that the dove was black, they indicate that the woman was Egyptian.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.57.

title.en: Melampus Learns the Phallos Procession in Egypt
title.zh: 墨蘭普斯在埃及習得陽具遊行

region.en: Egyptian villages and Boeotia (transmission of the Dionysos rites)
region.zh: 埃及村莊與玻俄提亞（狄俄倪索斯祭祀之傳播）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.48-49 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 48-49

summary.en: Egyptian women carry cubit-high dancing figures of Dionysos with movable phallos through the villages behind a flute, singing his praises — the rites, says Herodotus, that Melampus son of Amytheon learned in Egypt and taught to the Greeks, who thereafter carried the phallos in procession for Dionysos.
summary.zh: 埃及婦女攜一肘高之狄俄倪索斯舞像巡行村落，像之陽具以線操動，笛聲前導，頌歌隨行——希羅多德謂：墨蘭普斯習此於埃及，而後傳授希臘人，故希臘有陽具遊行之祭。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual-origin account via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Then for Dionysos on the eve of the festival each one kills a pig by cutting its throat before his own doors, and after that he gives the pig to the swineherd who sold it to him, to carry away again; and the rest of the feast of Dionysos is celebrated by the Egyptians in the same way as by the Hellenes in almost all things except choral dances, but instead of the phallos they have invented another contrivance, namely figures of about a cubit in height worked by strings, which women carry about the villages, with the privy member made to move and not much less in size than the rest of the body: and a flute goes before and they follow singing the praises of Dionysos.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.48.

passages.text: Now I think that Melampus the son of Amytheon was not without knowledge of these rites of sacrifice, but was acquainted with them: for Melampus is he who first set forth to the Hellenes the name of Dionysos and the manner of sacrifice and the procession of the phallos. Strictly speaking indeed, he when he made it known did not take in the whole, but those wise men who came after him made it known more at large. I say then that Melampus being a man of ability contrived for himself an art of divination, and having learnt from Egypt he taught the Hellenes many things, and among them those that concern Dionysos, making changes in some few points of them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.49.

title.en: The Phoenix Carries Its Father to the Temple of the Sun

region.en: Heliopolis, Egypt (temple of the Sun, where the phoenix appears)
region.zh: 埃及赫利奧波利斯（不死鳥顯現之日神廟）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.73 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 73

summary.en: The people of Heliopolis say the phoenix comes at intervals of five hundred years, when its father dies: partly gold-feathered and partly red, like an eagle in outline, it flies from Arabia bearing its father — plastered up in myrrh — to the temple of the Sun, and buries him there. Herodotus saw the bird only in painting, and says he cannot believe the story.
summary.zh: 赫利奧波利斯人言：不死鳥每五百年一至，值其父死時而來；羽半金半赤，形若鷹，自阿拉伯攜其父——以沒藥封裹——負至日神廟而葬之。希羅多德僅於畫中見之，自言未敢盡信。

sensitivity.note: Ancient wonder-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The Egyptian Bennu bird underlies the Greek phoenix.

passages.text: There is also another sacred bird called the phoenix which I did not myself see except in painting, for in truth he comes to them very rarely, at intervals, as the people of Heliopolis say, of five hundred years; and these say that he comes regularly when his father dies; and if he be like the painting, he is of this size and nature, that is to say, some of his feathers are of gold colour and others red, and in outline and size he is as nearly as possible like an eagle. This bird they say (but I cannot believe the story) contrives as follows: — setting forth from Arabia he conveys his father, they say, to the temple of the Sun plastered up in myrrh, and buries him in the temple of the Sun.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.73.

passages.text: And he conveys him thus: — he forms first an egg of myrrh as large as he is able to carry, and then he makes trial of carrying it, and when he has made trial sufficiently, then he hollows out the egg and places his father within it and plasters over with other myrrh that part of the egg where he hollowed it out to put his father in, and when his father is laid in it, it proves (they say) to be of the same weight as it was; and after he has plastered it up, he conveys the whole to Egypt to the temple of the Sun.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.73.

title.en: The Ibis and the Winged Serpents of Arabia

region.en: Mountain pass opposite Buto, edge of Egypt (where the ibis meets the flying serpents)
region.zh: 埃及邊境布托對面之山口（朱鷺迎擊飛蛇之地）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.75-76 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 75-76

summary.en: Each spring winged serpents fly from Arabia toward Egypt, and the ibises meet them at the narrow pass and kill them; heaps of their bones and spines cover the ground — the aition, Herodotus reports, of the ibis' great honour in Egypt, who saw the heaps himself and learned the tale from both Arabians and Egyptians.
summary.zh: 每歲春分，飛蛇自阿拉伯撲向埃及，朱鷺守狹口而擊殺之——蛇骨蛇棘遍堆於地，為埃及尊崇朱鷺之由。希羅多德自稱親見其堆，且此事得自阿拉伯人與埃及人兩方之口。

sensitivity.note: Ancient aition via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There is a region moreover in Arabia, situated nearly over against the city of Buto, to which place I came to inquire about the winged serpents: and when I came thither I saw bones of serpents and spines in quantity so great that it is impossible to make report of the number, and there were heaps of spines, some heaps large and others less large and others smaller still than these, and these heaps were many in number. This region in which the spines are scattered upon the ground is of the nature of an entrance from a narrow mountain pass to a great plain, which plain adjoins the plain of Egypt; and the story goes that at the beginning of spring winged serpents from Arabia fly towards Egypt, and the birds called ibises meet them at the entrance to this country and do not suffer the serpents to go by but kill them. On account of this deed it is (say the Arabians) that the ibis has come to be greatly honoured by the Egyptians, and the Egyptians also agree that it is for this reason that they honour these birds.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.75. / Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.75.

title.en: Sesostris the Conqueror: Pillars, Scythians, and the Fire of Daphnai
title.zh: 征服者塞索斯特里斯：石柱、斯基泰與達夫奈之火

region.en: From the Erythraian Sea to the Phasis (Sesostris' march; symbolic pin at Daphnai, Pelusium)
region.zh: 自紅海至法西斯河（塞索斯特里斯之遠征；象徵定位於達夫奈/佩魯西翁）

texts.period: Priests' account of an Old or New Kingdom conqueror, recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.102-110 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 102-110

summary.en: Sesostris sails the Erythraian Sea, marches over the continent setting up pillars — brave nations get his name, cowards get the emblem of a woman — until he crosses to Europe and subdues the Scythians; returning through Daphnai, his brother invites him to a feast and piles the house with brushwood; his wife counsels laying two of his six sons upon the pyre as a bridge, and the king escapes over their bodies while the brothers burn.
summary.zh: 塞索斯特里斯先航紅海，後率大軍征陸，凡遇勇敢死戰之國則立柱刻名，懦弱者則刻女陰以辱之；及至歐洲，降斯基泰而返。歸途達夫奈，其弟邀宴，積薪焚宅；其妻獻策：以二子伏火為橋，王履之而過，二子焚死，餘者得生。

sensitivity.note: Ancient heroic legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Egyptologists identify Sesostris with Senusret I/III or Ramesses II.

passages.text: Passing these by I shall make mention of the king who came after these, whose name was Sesostris. He (the priests said) first of all set out with ships of war from the Arabian gulf and subdued those who dwelt by the shores of the Erythraian Sea, until as he sailed he came to a sea which could no further be navigated by reason of shoals: then secondly, after he had returned to Egypt, according to the report of the priests he took a great army and marched over the continent, subduing every nation which stood in his way: and those of them whom he found valiant and fighting desperately for their freedom, in their lands he set up pillars ...; but as to those of whose cities he obtained possession without fighting or with ease, on their pillars he inscribed words after the same tenor as he did for the nations which had shown themselves courageous, and in addition he drew upon them the hidden parts of a woman, desiring to signify by this that the people were cowards and effeminate.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.102, condensed with ellipsis; not verbatim throughout.

passages.text: Thus doing he traversed the continent, until at last he passed over to Europe from Asia and subdued the Scythians and also the Thracians. These, I am of opinion, were the furthest people to which the Egyptian army came, for in their country the pillars are found to have been set up, but in the land beyond this they are no longer found.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.103.

passages.text: As this Egyptian Sesostris was returning and bringing back many men of the nations whose lands he had subdued, when he came (said the priests) to Daphnai in the district of Pelusion on his journey home, his brother to whom Sesostris had entrusted the charge of Egypt invited him and with him his sons to a feast; and then he piled the house round with brushwood and set it on fire: and Sesostris when he discovered this forthwith took counsel with his wife, for he was bringing with him (they said) his wife also; and she counselled him to lay out upon the pyre two of his sons, which were six in number, and so to make a bridge over the burning mass, and that they passing over their bodies should thus escape. This, they said, Sesostris did, and two of his sons were burnt to death in this manner, but the rest got away safe with their father.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.107.

title.en: Pheros Casts His Spear into the River: Ten Years Blind
title.zh: 斐羅斯擲矛入河：十年失明

region.en: The Nile in flood and the temple of the Sun, Heliopolis (Pheros' obelisks)
region.zh: 泛濫之尼羅與赫利奧波利斯日神廟（斐羅斯方尖碑）

texts.period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.111 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 111

summary.en: In his eighteenth-cubit flood year, King Pheros in presumptuous folly hurls a spear into the eddies of the Nile and goes blind for ten years; the oracle of Buto promises sight if he washes his eyes with the tears of a woman faithful to her own husband — tested wife by wife until one cures him — and the king burns the faithless women alive in the city of Erythrabolos and weds the faithful one.
summary.zh: 尼羅漲至十八肘之歲，王斐羅斯愚妄投矛於漩流，遂盲十年；布托神諭許之：以忠於其夫之婦人之淚洗目可復明——逐一試之，至一婦而愈——王遂於埃里特拉波羅斯城焚諸不貞之婦，娶其貞者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-legend via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Now after Sesostris had brought his life to an end, his son Pheros, they told me, received in succession the kingdom, and he made no warlike expedition, and moreover it chanced to him to become blind by reason of the following accident: — when the river had come down in flood rising to a height of eighteen cubits, higher than ever before that time, and had gone over the fields, a wind fell upon it and the river became agitated by waves: and this king (they say) moved by presumptuous folly took a spear and cast it into the midst of the eddies of the stream; and immediately upon this he had a disease of the eyes and was by it made blind.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.111.

passages.text: For ten years then he was blind, and in the eleventh year there came to him an oracle from the city of Buto saying that the time of his punishment had expired, and that he should see again if he washed his eyes with the water of a woman who had accompanied with her own husband only and had not knowledge of other men: and first he made trial of his own wife, and then, as he continued blind, he went on to try all the women in turn; and when he had at last regained his sight he gathered together all the women of whom he had made trial, excepting her by whose means he had regained his sight, to one city which now is named Erythrabolos, and having gathered them to this he consumed them all by fire, as well as the city itself; but as for her by whose means he had regained his sight, he had her himself to wife.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.111.

passages.text: Then after he had escaped the malady of his eyes he dedicated offerings at each one of the temples which were of renown, and especially (to mention only that which is most worthy of mention) he dedicated at the temple of the Sun works which are worth seeing, namely two obelisks of stone, each of a single block, measuring in length a hundred cubits each one and in breadth eight cubits.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.111.

title.en: Helen in Egypt: The Judgment of King Proteus at Memphis
title.zh: 海倫在埃及：孟菲斯王普羅透斯之審

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (the enclosure of Proteus and the temple of the foreign Aphrodite)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（普羅透斯聖域與異邦阿佛洛狄忒神廟）

texts.period: Priests' account recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.112-116 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, secs. 112-116

summary.en: The Egyptian counter-story to the Trojan War: winds drove Alexander (Paris) and Helen to Egypt, where his slaves fled to the asylum of the temple of Heracles and accused him; King Proteus of Memphis summoned the seducer, condemned him — 'thou didst go in to the wife of thine own host' — kept Helen and the treasure for Menelaos, and sent Paris empty away; Herodotus swears Homer knew this version and turned from it.
summary.zh: 特洛伊戰爭之埃及異聞：風將帕里斯與海倫吹至埃及，其僕逃入赫拉克勒斯神廟聖域而發其罪；孟菲斯王普羅透斯召而審之——『汝通主母』——奪海倫與財留還墨涅拉俄斯，逐帕里斯空手而歸；希羅多德斷言荷馬知此說而捨之。

sensitivity.note: Ancient myth via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Cross-tradition link: the Egyptian Helen episode behind Stesichorus' palinode and Euripides' Helen.

passages.text: After him, they said, there succeeded to the throne a man of Memphis, whose name in the tongue of the Hellenes was Proteus; for whom there is now a sacred enclosure at Memphis, very fair and well ordered, lying on that side of the temple of Hephaistos which faces the North Wind. Round about this enclosure dwell Phenicians of Tyre, and this whole region is called the Camp of the Tyrians. Within the enclosure of Proteus there is a temple called the temple of the 'foreign Aphrodite,' which temple I conjecture to be one of Helen the daughter of Tyndareus, not only because I have heard the tale how Helen dwelt with Proteus, but also especially because it is called by the name of the 'foreign Aphrodite.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.112.

passages.text: And the priests told me, when I inquired, that the things concerning Helen happened thus: — Alexander having carried off Helen was sailing away from Sparta to his own land, and when he had come to the Egean Sea contrary winds drove him from his course to the Sea of Egypt; and after that, since the blasts did not cease to blow, he came to Egypt itself, and in Egypt to that which is now named the Canobic mouth of the Nile and to Taricheiai. Now there was upon the shore, as still there is now, a temple of Heracles, in which if any man's slave take refuge and have the sacred marks set upon him, giving himself over to the god, it is not lawful to lay hands upon him.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.113.

passages.text: At length Proteus declared to them this sentence, saying, 'Were it not that I count it a matter of great moment not to slay any of those strangers who being driven from their course by winds have come to my land hitherto, I should have taken vengeance on thee on behalf of the man of Hellas, seeing that thou, most base of men, having received from him hospitality, didst work against him a most impious deed. For thou didst go in to the wife of thine own host; and even this was not enough for thee, but thou didst stir her up with desire and hast gone away with her like a thief.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.115.

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (the stone treasury of the king)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（王者石室寶庫）

texts.period: Priests' tale recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.121 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 121

summary.en: The treasury's own builder leaves his sons a removable stone; the thief caught in a trap sends his brother to cut off his head, the mother forces the survivor to reclaim the corpse, the guards are made drunk on wine-skins and shaved in mockery, and finally — at the king's own daughter's stews — the thief, clutching a dead man's arm in the dark, confesses his two crimes and escapes, winning pardon, a great reward, and the king's daughter.
summary.zh: 寶庫建造者臨終授子以可移之石；兄落阱，弟受命斷其首；母迫生者索還屍身——以酒囊灌醉守衛、剃其右頰以嘲之；末至王女之室，暗中持死人臂以代己，自陳兩樁罪——王服其智，赦而賞之，並以其女妻焉。

sensitivity.note: Ancient folk-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. One of the oldest recorded trickster-cycle tales in world literature.

passages.text: This king, they said, got great wealth of silver, which none of the kings born after him could surpass or even come near to; and wishing to store his wealth in safety he caused to be built a chamber of stone, one of the walls whereof was towards the outside of his palace: and the builder of this, having a design against it, contrived as follows, that is, he disposed one of the stones in such a manner that it could be taken out easily from the wall either by two men or even by one. So when the chamber was finished, the king stored his money in it, and after some time the builder, being near the end of his life, called to him his sons (for he had two) and to them he related how he had contrived in building the treasury of the king, and all in forethought for them, that they might have ample means of living.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.121(a).

passages.text: When the thieves had come as at former times and one of them had entered, then so soon as he came near to one of the vessels he was straightway caught in the trap: and when he perceived in what evil case he was, straightway calling his brother he showed him what the matter was, and bade him enter as quickly as possible and cut off his head, for fear lest being seen and known he might bring about the destruction of his brother also. And to the other it seemed that he spoke well, and he was persuaded and did so; and fitting the stone into its place he departed home bearing with him the head of his brother.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.121(b-c).

passages.text: He contrived for his purpose a device as follows: — Providing himself with asses he filled some skins with wine and laid them upon the asses, and after that he drove them along: and when he came opposite to those who were guarding the corpse hung up, he drew towards him two or three of the necks of the skins and loosened the cords with which they were tied... and in the end he made them a present of one of the skins in addition to what they had. Upon that they lay down there without more ado, being minded to drink... Then as it was now far on in the night, he first took down the body of his brother, and then in mockery shaved the right cheeks of all the guards; and after that he put the dead body upon the asses and drove them away home.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.121(d).

passages.text: He caused his own daughter to sit in the stews, and enjoined her to receive all equally, and before having commerce with any one to compel him to tell her what was the most cunning and what the most unholy deed which had been done by him in all his life-time... the thief, hearing for what purpose this was done and having a desire to get the better of the king in resource, did thus: — from the body of one lately dead he cut off the arm at the shoulder and went with it under his mantle: and having gone in to the daughter of the king, and being asked that which the others also were asked, he related that he had done the most unholy deed when he cut off the head of his brother... and she when she heard it tried to take hold of him, but the thief held out to her in the darkness the arm of the corpse... but the thief left it in her hands and departed, escaping through the door. Rhampsinitos greatly marvelled at him, and gave him this daughter of his to wife, counting him to be the most knowing of all men.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.121(e-f).

title.en: Rhampsinitos Plays Dice with Demeter in Hades
title.zh: 拉美西尼圖斯冥府與得墨忒爾擲骰

region.en: The temple of Demeter, twenty furlongs from the city (symbolic pin, Egyptian underworld journey)
region.zh: 距城二十弗隆之地母神廟（象徵定位，埃及冥府之旅）

texts.period: Priests' tale recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.122 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 122

summary.en: After the thief's pardon, King Rhampsinitos went down alive to the place the Greeks call Hades, played dice with Demeter, sometimes winning and sometimes losing, and returned bearing a gift of a handkerchief of gold; ever after, at the feast of his descent, the priests weave a robe in a single day, blindfold one of their number, and two wolves lead the blind priest twenty furlongs to the temple of Demeter and back again.
summary.zh: 神偷既赦，王拉美西尼圖斯生入希臘人所稱冥府，與得墨忒爾擲骰，互有勝負，懷其金帕而返；自是其降冥之日成節：祭司一日織成一袍，蒙其一目，兩狼引之二十弗隆至地母廟，復引之而歸。

sensitivity.note: Ancient underworld-visit tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Cluster: descent to the underworld.

passages.text: After these things they said this king went down alive to that place which by the Hellenes is called Hades, and there played at dice with Demeter, and in some throws he overcame her and in others he was overcome by her; and he came back again having as a gift from her a handkerchief of gold: and they told me that because of the going down of Rhampsinitos the Egyptians after he came back celebrated a feast, which I know of my own knowledge also that they still observe even to my time; but whether it is for this cause that they keep the feast or for some other, I am not able to say.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.122.

passages.text: However, the priests weave a robe completely on the very day of the feast, and forthwith they bind up the eyes of one of them with a fillet, and having led him with the robe to the way by which one goes to the temple of Demeter, they depart back again themselves. This priest, they say, with his eyes bound up is led by two wolves to the temple of Demeter, which is distant from the city twenty furlongs, and then afterwards the wolves lead him back again from the temple to the same spot.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.122.

title.en: The Soul's Round of Three Thousand Years

region.en: Egypt, land of the first doctrine of the immortal soul (symbolic pin, Thebes)
region.zh: 埃及，不死靈魂之說首傳之地（象徵定位，底比斯）

texts.period: Priests' doctrine recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.123 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 123

summary.en: Herodotus records the Egyptian doctrine that the soul of man is immortal: at death it enters another creature coming to birth, and after passing through all creatures of land, sea, and air, enters a human body again — a round of three thousand years; certain Greeks, he notes pointedly, adopted the doctrine 'as if it were their own invention.'
summary.zh: 希羅多德錄埃及之教：人之靈魂不死——身死而魂入新生之物，遍歷陸海空萬類之後，復入人身，其輪迴之期為三千年；並譏某希臘人襲取此說而自詡為其發明。

sensitivity.note: Ancient doctrinal report via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The doctrine is the Pythagorean-Orphic transmigration in its Egyptian source-form.

passages.text: The Egyptians say that Demeter and Dionysos are rulers of the world below; and the Egyptians are also the first who reported the doctrine that the soul of man is immortal, and that when the body dies, the soul enters into another creature which chances then to be coming to the birth, and when it has gone the round of all the creatures of land and sea and of the air, it enters again into a human body as it comes to the birth; and that it makes this round in a period of three thousand years. This doctrine certain Hellenes adopted, some earlier and some later, as if it were of their own invention, and of these men I know the names but I abstain from recording them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.123. / Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.123.
